title: Lester sits in for Hawkins with Fletcher Henderson
summary: Phillips says Lester took Hawkins's place with Henderson after Herschel Evans was afraid to; people in Kansas City called him Red, and Lester said he refused to copy Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: That's interesting. King Oliver said he liked him, and he told Red Allen about him.

And when he got to Kansas City, Fletcher Henderson picked him. Hawk had left and went home'. See, he lived in St. Joseph, about 35-40 miles away from Kansas City. So he went over there, and Fletcher Henderson was asking could he get a tenor player to play for him that night in Hawkins' place. Herschel said...

Yeah. Prez told Herschel, "Why don't you go and make it, Herschel?" Herschel said, "No, man, I can't make it." Herschel didn't read too good. He said, "You'all make it." They called him Red. They didn't call him Prez in Kansas City; they called him Red.
Why did they call him that?
Well, because of his color,m I guess. "Say, Red..." You never did see Lester.
Well, I've seen pictures. Did he have any Indian blood in him maybe?

I don't know. His mother was a black-skinned lady. Maybe she had something like that. But he was red. He was Morinie(?) Red. That's what we called him. Then we called Red Elkins "Kentucky Red." There was two Reds in the band. Anyway...
So you were talking about Prez talking to Herschel and telling him...

Yeah. He said, "You scared to go, man" -- to Herschel. Herschel said, "Yeah, man, I'm scared." Fletcher Henderson, you know, had a hell of a name in those days. Prez said, "I ain't scared, man. I'll go there." So he went there and played that night with him -- Fletcher sent for him. Hawk left for about a month, something like that. Then Hawk left and went to Europe, so Fletcher sent for him, and he came I think he stayed for three or four months, something like that.

He told me, man, "Them changes they wanted me to go through, Phil." He said, "I couldn't go sittin' down and learnin' somebody's solos. Ain't that a bitch? Imagine me! And I got my style of playing. Tryin' to play like somebody else. I don't want to play like Hawk or nobody else. I want to play like me." I said, "Yeah, that's right, man. You don't have to be copyin' nobody. Not you. Because you know good and well..." We traveled all over the country practically. And we never ran into nobody played saxophone like he did.
